transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-26
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (scheduled)
Recording: Fireflies (auto)
Attendees: Priya Shah (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Leo Martinez (Redwood CSM); Jordan Hayes (CTO), Maya Patel (Platform Eng), Evan Cole (SRE), Rita Gomez (Security)

Summary (auto):
Cottontree is evaluating Redwood for low-latency streaming user-facing features and high-concurrency batch embeddings. Primary concerns are p95 latency for streaming tokens, steady-state token/sec throughput, and isolation (VPC vs hosted). They requested pricing, SOC2/KMS docs, and a benchmark window.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency shapes, streaming vs sync, token/sec microbenchmarks, hosting modes (hosted/dedicated/private), security controls (KMS, SSO), rollout/fallback plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Priya Shah: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm priya from redwood, alex is out today so i'm your AE. quick introductions?
[00:08] Jordan Hayes: jordan here, cto at cottontree, maya is on infra, evan handles sres, rita is security. thanks for squeezing us in.
[00:16] Priya Shah: awesome. daniel from our se team is joining to get into the numbers. daniel, want to say hi?
[00:22] Daniel Kim: yeah hi, daniel kim, solutions eng. i'll be driving the perf notes and the benchmark plan. quick note — we'll probably use a token/sec microbenchmark and a streaming p95 trace to match your app.
[00:34] Maya Patel: great. to give context, our app is real-time doc summarization in the browser, users expect streaming highlights while they scroll. target p95 ideally <120ms per token with streaming turned on for short responses (200-400 tokens), and for longer background jobs we do batch generation.
[00:50] Evan Cole: concurrency is a big one for us — we see spikes to ~750 concurrent sessions during peak, sustained 250-300 typical. average request length is 350 tokens but distribution heavy on short responses (like 50-150 tokens).
[01:08] Rita Gomez: security: we need SOC2 Type II, KMS integration (our cloud KMS), SSO via SAML, RBAC and audit loqs — and we want data residency in eu-west for eu customers.
[01:28] Priya Shah: thanks, that's super helpful. quick check — are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private at this point?
[01:35] Jordan Hayes: leaning hosted to start because speed of onboarding matters, but we need guarantees on lat and a path to dedicated if costs or isolation become an issue.
[01:45] Priya Shah: totally reasonable. our hosted plan can hit low p95s for streaming, we have a model catalog and burst capacity — but dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable tail lat. daniel can walk through kernels/batching tradeoffs.
[01:58] Daniel Kim: yes — some of the knobs: quantization profiles, continuous batching, prefix caching (we call KV cache, sometimes the transcription shows KV cash lol), and kernel selection per model. for streaming p95 under 120ms we typically recommend a compact model or deduped prompt shapes, plus a dedicated pool if sustained concurrency is high.
[02:20] Maya Patel: you mentioned prefix caching — how often does that actually help for short streaming sessions? our requests are mostly new context per user so prefix reuse is low.
[02:31] Daniel Kim: if prefix reuse is low, caching less helpful, so batching and kernel latency matter most. for short responses, the per-token overhead (scheduler hops, tokenization, network) dominates. our runtime tries to keep kv cache hot and batch multiple small inferences when helpful but there's a latency tradeoff.
[02:49] Jordan Hayes: can you give a rough cost vs latency tradeoff? hosted vs dedicated?
[02:55] Priya Shah: rough rule: hosted is lower operational overhead and flexible burst, but at high steady-state throughput dedicated often gives 25-40% unit cost reduction and more consistent p95s. exact numbers depend on model size and sequence length. we'll share a pricing matrix after the call.
[03:12] Rita Gomez: for security, can hosted meet our KMS+SAML needs, or does private required?
[03:18] Priya Shah: hosted supports KMS integrations and SAML SSO via a private customer-configured auth layer. for strict network isolation or air-gapped needs, Private (VPC/on-prem) is the path. we also have SOC2 artifacts we can share.
[03:31] Evan Cole: what about cold starts — if we route to a different region or fallback to another model, how do you keep p95s reasonable?
[03:38] Daniel Kim: we use smart routing and warm standby pools; for critical routes we recommend pinning model variants and using canary rollouts rather than on-the-fly fallback. cold starts can add 100-500ms depending on model and hardware.
[03:50] Maya Patel: for our traffic patterns, we need a p95 SLA for the streaming path. is that something Redwood will commit to in hosted?
[03:58] Priya Shah: hosted has latency SLOs on premium plans; Dedicated gives contractual SLAs with reserved capacity. We can map your target (<120ms p95 for streaming tokens) to an offering and show historical percentiles from similar customers.
[04:12] Jordan Hayes: ok, i'd like to see a historical p95 sample from a similar deployment — can you show an example?
[04:18] Daniel Kim: yes — i'll attach a dashboard snapshot and a short CSV with p50/p90/p95 distribution across token positions. note, the model and seq length strongly change the numbers.
[04:29] Priya Shah: quick qualification — what's your timeline for a pilot?
[04:33] Jordan Hayes: ideally 2-3 weeks to validate latency/cost, then decision within a month.
[04:38] Priya Shah: great. we'll propose a 3-hour microbenchmark window for the spike tests and a day for longer soak tests.
[04:45] Evan Cole: for benchmarks, what does Redwood need from us?
[04:49] Daniel Kim: sample traffic shape (percent short vs long, concurrency curve), an API key for the sandbox, and any network constraints. we can run tests from our hosted infra or coordinate with your VPC if you prefer private endpoints.
[05:03] Maya Patel: i'm worried about token/sec at scale — we do bursts up to 15k tokens/sec across the fleet for a minute during promotions. can you sustain that without degrading p95?
[05:12] Daniel Kim: burst sustain depends on model and pooled capacity. for short bursts, hosted can borrow burst capacity but p95 may increase slightly; Dedicated reserved pools prevent noisy neighbor effects and keep p95 stable. we often recommend a hybrid: hosted with committed capacity for baseline and burst credits for promotions.
[05:31] Priya Shah: i'd like to surface an example math: if you need 15k token/s sustained for 60s on a Llama-style model at 4-bit quant, that might map to N GPUs in dedicated; we'll calculate GPUs and show estimated unit cost.
[05:44] Jordan Hayes: that'd be helpful. also curious about streaming token latency vs truncation — we sometimes emit tokens in sub-second batches, will Redwood's streaming chunking introduce latency?
[05:55] Daniel Kim: our streaming supports immediate token pushes and configurable chunk sizes; network RTT still matters. for browser clients we recommend small chunks with websocket streaming and client-side assembly.
[06:09] Rita Gomez: about compliance, we'll need audit logs per user action, retention policies, and encryption in transit and at rest. can you confirm data retention controls?
[06:19] Priya Shah: yes, we have retention policies configurable per-tenant and audit logs accessible via console + exported to your SIEM. we support encryption at rest (customer-managed keys with KMS) and in transit. we'll attach our security pack.
[06:34] Maya Patel: minor thing — what's your metric for p95 measurement? is it per-token, or per-response?
[06:40] Daniel Kim: good question. for streaming p95 we often measure per-token generation latency (time between request and token arrival). for request-level p95 we measure end-to-end response completion. we'll align with your definition for the benchmark.
[06:55] Jordan Hayes: what's the overhead of switching to a newer model version mid-rollout? can we do canary at 5% traffic?
[07:02] Daniel Kim: yes, we support canaries and A/B rollouts with traffic split; KV cache warming is something to watch, you may see transient latency shifts during switchovers. we have an auto-fallback policy to go back if errors or p95 regress.
[07:17] Priya Shah: can i ask about your success criteria — aside from the <120ms p95 — what else matters for go/no-go?
[07:24] Jordan Hayes: cost per 1k tokens, predictability during bursts, and security posture are top. plus an integration timeline that fits our marketing sprint (4 weeks).
[07:36] Priya Shah: perfect. we'll tailor the benchmark to measure cost per token at target latency and show tradeoffs.
[07:43] Maya Patel: one more technical — are there kernel-level optimizations for kv cache eviction to help long conversations? we have some stateful sessions.
[07:53] Daniel Kim: yes, our runtime has eviction heuristics and small kv caching optimizations; for long convos, we recommend a combination of truncation + external context store. some of the terms in our docs get mangled in transcriptions, like kernel vs colonel sometimes, so we'll send a clarified infra note.
[08:12] Jordan Hayes: ok, so next steps we'd like: pricing, SOC2 + KMS docs, and a benchmark slot. also show a sample SLO in hosted vs dedicated.
[08:21] Priya Shah: noted — we'll send pricing and security docs in the next 48 hours and propose benchmark windows for next week. daniel will own the plan.
[08:29] Leo Martinez: just flagging we'll include a short onboarding checklist and a sandbox API key request form.
[08:36] Maya Patel: can we get the sandbox with eu-west endpoints?
[08:40] Daniel Kim: yes, we'll provision sandbox endpoints in eu-west for you.
[08:44] Rita Gomez: also please include the encryption-at-rest flow for customer-managed keys — want the KMS flow doc.
[08:51] Priya Shah: will do.
[09:00] Jordan Hayes: anything else on the performance side?
[09:03] Daniel Kim: just that for the microbenchmark we'll measure token/sec, p50/p90/p95 token latency, and sample concurrency curves. we'll also do short soak runs to look for tail degradation.
[09:16] Maya Patel: good. for the soak runs, can we run a 12-hour test passing our real-ish workload?
[09:22] Daniel Kim: yep, that's part of the deeper POC once initial spikes look good.
[09:27] Priya Shah: recap: deliverables from Redwood — pricing matrix, SOC2/KMS docs, benchmark plan + proposed windows; deliverables from Cottontree — traffic shape and acceptance criteria.
[09:39] Jordan Hayes: correct. we'll aim to provide traffic shape by Tuesday.
[09:44] Priya Shah: perfect. any final questions?
[09:47] Rita Gomez: one quick — do you offer per-route token-level cost breakdown in console?
[09:53] Leo Martinez: yes, per-route cost and latency per token is in console on our premium tier; we can demo in the next call.
[10:01] Jordan Hayes: ok great. thanks everyone.
[10:05] Priya Shah: thanks — we'll follow up with docs and benchmark times.
